The proposed solution is incorrect. 

A simple counterexample shows that a density much larger than $1/2^r$ is always achievable:
Consider the set of all $S$-smooth integers where the exponent of $p_1$ is odd. For any $n$ in this set, $p_1 n$ has an even exponent of $p_1$ and therefore cannot belong to the set. Consequently, this set cannot contain both $n$ and $p_1 n$, so it avoids the configuration $\{n, p_1 n, \dots, p_r n\}$ entirely. The asymptotic density of this set is $1/2$, which strictly exceeds $1/2^r$ for all $r \ge 2$.

The proposed solution incorrectly equates avoiding the full configuration $\{n, p_1 n, \dots, p_r n\}$ (a hyperedge of size $r+1$) with finding an independent set in a graph where each configuration forms a clique (which would forbid sharing even two elements).

VERDICT: REJECT
